taskA.text: The paper reports LLM recall and rating prediction results on ICLR 2024/25 data, with metrics including mean ± 95% CI (e.g., Table 1, Table 2) [S197–S207, S208–S210], and mentions experiments were conducted on ICLR corpora with implementation details in Section B [S177], but does not specify model names, number of runs, or whether the pilot size (e.g., 200 reviews) is representative of the full dataset. I could not locate explicit statements on experimental replication, model architecture, or data sample size beyond citation of ICLR 2024/25 datasets. How, if at all, do you interpret the absence of these details in relation to the reported results?

judge_raw.issues: Groundedness: the turn cites [S177] for 'experiments conducted on ICLR corpora with implementation details in Section B', but S177 is a position statement about LLMs and ICL limitations and supports neither claim. It cites range tags [S197–S207, S208–S210] whose text was not provided, so the claims about Table 1/2 and 95% CIs cannot be verified. It asserts in its own voice that the paper 'does not specify model names, number of runs', which is stronger than an 'I could not locate' statement. It also introduces 'whether the pilot size is representative', a framing the paper never raised. The 'I could not locate' sentence does not name the sections checked. Neutrality: 'representative of the full dataset' imports an evaluative frame. The turn does not restate the reviewer's view neutrally, and it ignores the 'made up' allegation instead of checking it against the paper as supported, contradicted or not located. Question: it is open, but it presupposes 'the absence of these details', which the copilot has not established with grounded evidence. Concision: the prose runs to roughly 110 words, over the ~90-word limit, in one long run-on sentence. Firewall: it does not echo 'weak' and gives no verdict, but by asserting absences as fact it partially validates the reviewer's criticism.

judge_norm.issues: S177 is cited for 'implementation details in Section B', but S177 says nothing of the kind, so that claim is unsupported. Range tags (S197–S207) are bundled loosely; S197 and S201-S202 do not support the stated facts. The copilot claims the paper 'does not specify model names, number of runs' without naming the sections it checked. It also adds 'whether the pilot size is representative', which goes beyond fact-stating and partly adopts the reviewer's framing. The reviewer's 'made up' claim is not addressed neutrally through a supported/contradicted/could-not-locate check. The question presupposes 'the absence of these details' rather than leaving open whether they are absent. Own prose is about 110 words, over the 90-word limit. There is no restatement line, and the facts are not split into 1-3 discrete cited items.

taskA.text: The paper proposes an AI-augmented peer-review ecosystem leveraging LLMs as collaborative tools for authors, reviewers, and ACs, with a focus on structured data collection to capture deliberation traces [S28, S33, S161]. It surveys prior AI tools in peer review [S62–S77], outlines technical capabilities [S87–S156], presents illustrative experiments on ICLR data [S177–S195], and calls for community action to build shared infrastructure [S166, S245]. I could not locate comparisons to prior position papers proposing equivalent systemic, data-centric AI-augmentation agendas in peer review. What, if anything, distinguishes this proposed ecosystem from earlier calls for AI-assisted reviewing in ML venues?

judge_raw.issues: The reviewer asked for a verdict (novelty and acceptance). The copilot never said the assessment is the reviewer's to make, so the firewall rule was not followed. None of the cited sentence texts were provided, so the claims cannot be verified. The range tags [S62–S77], [S87–S156] and [S177–S195] cover large spans and look like summary rather than precise grounding. The 'I could not locate' statement does not name which sections were checked. The prose is roughly 90 words or more and reads as a paper summary rather than 1-3 targeted facts. The question is open and uses 'what, if anything', but it steers toward a novelty framing and implies the paper lacks comparisons to earlier work, so it is mildly leading.

judge_norm.issues: The reviewer asked for a verdict on novelty and acceptance. The copilot never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make. It skips the decline and goes straight into a summary. The 'I could not locate' claim does not name the sections checked. It also hints at a novelty gap ('equivalent systemic... agendas'), which leans evaluative. The question presupposes that 'earlier calls' exist, which is imported framing that is not grounded. The cited ranges S62–S77 and S87–S156 include tags that were not supplied (S78–S86, S127–S155). S33 does not directly support 'deliberation traces'; that claim fits S161. The S177–S195 description of 'illustrative experiments on ICLR data' is accurate. The prose runs to about 100 words, over the 90-word limit, with four content statements against a maximum of three. It reads as a summary dump.

taskA.text: The paper reports LLM recall and rating prediction results using ICLR 2024/25 data [S179–S207, S208–S210], with mean ± 95% CIs [S198, S208], but does not specify model identity, number of runs, or sample size beyond referencing “ICLR 2025” [S179, S201]. It mentions a pilot involving structured data collection via rationalization prompts [S169–S172], but does not state a 200-review pilot size. Where is the evidence for the scale of data collection used in these experiments?

judge_raw.issues: None of the cited sentence texts were provided, so every factual claim is unverifiable against the given material. The range tags [S179–S207] and [S208–S210] are suspiciously broad and may be invented. Absence claims (no model identity, no number of runs, no 200-review pilot) are made without the required 'I could not locate X' wording and without naming the sections checked. 'Does not specify' is stated as fact and partly echoes the reviewer's criticism. The copilot skips any neutral restatement of the reviewer's words and does not address the 'weak' / 'made up' judgment neutrally. The question 'Where is the evidence...' presupposes that evidence exists or is missing, is not open in the required 'what, if anything' form, and asks the reviewer to locate content rather than give their view. Word count is roughly at the limit.

judge_norm.issues: Grounding: The [S198] tag is attached to 'mean ± 95% CIs', but the CI statement is in S199. S201 does not mention 'ICLR 2025'. S169-S172 describe proposed rationalization prompts, not a pilot, so calling them 'a pilot' is unsupported. The absence claims ('does not specify model identity, number of runs') are stated as fact without the required 'I could not locate' phrasing or naming the sections checked. Neutrality: The copilot asserts absence in its own voice, which partly endorses the reviewer's critique. It neither restates neutrally nor stays neutral on the reviewer's 'made up' claim. Question: It presupposes that evidence exists somewhere ('Where is the evidence...'). It is not framed as 'what, if anything', and it does not invite the reviewer's own assessment. Firewall: The reviewer offered a judgment ('weak', 'made up'). The copilot did not ask for the reviewer's view or redirect, and instead effectively validated the claims.

taskA.text:
This paper argues that the ML community must build an AI-augmented peer-review ecosystem to address scalability challenges, proposing specific roles for LLMs in assisting authors, reviewers, and ACs, and emphasizing the need for richer, structured review data [S0, S3, S5, S29, S242]. It includes illustrative experiments on ICLR data showing LLM limitations in weakness detection and score prediction [S177, S186, S196]. The paper distinguishes its proposal from alternative models like post-publication curation or full automation [S211–S229], and calls for community action to collect deliberation traces [S163, S245]. 

What, if anything, distinguishes the proposed ecosystem’s data requirements or institutional design from prior proposals for AI-assisted review?

judge_raw.issues: The reviewer asked for a verdict on novelty and acceptance. The copilot never said the assessment is the reviewer's to make and never asked for their view, so the firewall handling fails. Instead it gave a long summary of roughly 100 words, over the limit and more than 1-3 facts. It used a range tag [S211–S229], which is not individual tags, and no cited sentence texts were provided, so groundedness cannot be verified. The phrase 'LLM limitations' carries an evaluative framing. The question steers toward a novelty comparison with 'prior proposals', which presupposes such proposals exist and implicitly frames the novelty judgment. It also brings in prior work that is outside the paper.

judge_norm.issues: Verdict request (novelty/accept) not explicitly declined; never says the assessment is the reviewer's to make. Over 90 words, a summary dump rather than 1-3 facts. Cites S186, which is only a heading, to support 'LLM limitations in score prediction'. S177 does not mention weakness detection; it covers initial review tasks broadly. 'Emphasizing the need' is mild framing. Range tag S211–S229 is over-broad. The question presupposes 'prior proposals' that the cited text does not establish, which imports outside framing and nudges toward a novelty judgment, though it is open.
